profiles.meeting_scenario: At a 350-bed U.S. teaching hospital, a newly formed diagnostic safety committee has flagged three delayed lung cancer diagnoses involving incidental pulmonary nodules first seen on emergency department chest CTs. The cases surfaced during a review prompted by the hospital's broader response to National Academy of Medicine recommendations on diagnostic error. This troubleshooting meeting brings together the ED quality lead and the radiology incidental findings coordinator to figure out why the current follow-up process failed despite both services believing a safety net was already in place. The agenda is to compare the recent cases, identify where the process broke down, and choose an immediate workflow fix to test next month. The expected outcome is a shared action plan for handling incidental nodules from ED imaging, including who owns the next step after the scan is read.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Emergency diagnosis, discharge workflows, peer-review of return visits, and ED documentation improvement
members.background: Board-certified emergency physician with 12 years in practice; now spends part of her time on ED quality and patient safety after several years as assistant medical director.
members.private_state: She wants a fix that reduces missed diagnoses without adding a heavy new burden to ED physicians at discharge, and she is wary of the issue being framed as an ED diagnostic failure when the abnormality was already identified on imaging.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'follow-up was arranged,' that usually means the discharge paperwork told the patient to see their primary care clinician or a specialist, not that a downstream appointment was actually scheduled.
The 'March nodule list' naturally refers to patients discharged from the ED in March, because ED quality reviews are organized by visit month.
A 'high-risk' nodule case means a patient with strong clinical cancer risk factors such as smoking history, prior malignancy, or weight loss.
If the ED places any outpatient referral related to the finding before discharge, the case has effectively been handed off out of the ED workflow.

members.name: Karen Wu, RN
members.expertise: Imaging result communication, radiology follow-up registries, Fleischner guideline workflows, and patient outreach for incidental findings
members.background: Registered nurse who previously worked in pulmonary clinic care coordination and now manages the health system's registry for incidental lung nodules identified on radiology reports.
members.private_state: She wants to show that radiology's tracking program works when cases enter it correctly, and she is concerned the real failure is that ED cases never reached the registry or used the dedicated referral pathway.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'follow-up was arranged,' that means the patient was entered into the nodule registry and either contacted or given a booked imaging or clinic plan.
The 'March nodule list' refers to radiology reports finalized in March, regardless of when the patient physically visited the ED.
A 'high-risk' nodule case means the guideline-based high-risk category used in radiology recommendations, which is not identical to a clinician's broader cancer-risk impression.
Only the specific incidental lung nodule referral order routes the case into the registry; a generic pulmonology or PCP referral does not count as entering the formal follow-up pathway.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'close the loop'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the goal is to make sure incidental nodules are 'followed up' and that the team 'closes the loop.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the loop is closed when the ED documents the finding, tells the patient to seek outpatient care, and places an appropriate referral or recommendation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the loop is closed only when the case enters the radiology tracking pathway and there is confirmed outreach, scheduling, or registry-based surveillance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In diagnostic safety work, 'close the loop' is a standard phrase with a shared positive meaning, so both hear alignment and do not pause to unpack whether the endpoint is documentation, handoff, or actual appointment capture.

misalignment_points.topic: Which cases are in the 'March nodule list'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to reviewing 'the March cases' or 'the March nodule list.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of ED encounters that occurred and were discharged in March.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of CT reports finalized by radiology in March, including scans from late February that crossed over after overnight reads.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both services routinely organize work by month, and 'March list' sounds concrete enough that neither notices they are indexing different operational timestamps.

misalignment_points.topic: Who counts as a 'high-risk' nodule patient
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'high-risk patients' should never be missed.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means patients with obvious clinical red flags or major cancer history, the ones an ED physician would intuitively view as urgent.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means patients meeting the radiology guideline's high-risk category for nodule surveillance recommendations, even if they do not appear alarming during the ED visit.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'high-risk' feels medically standard, but its practical threshold differs by setting; each assumes the other is using the same accepted meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'putting in the order' actually routes to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the ED should 'put the order in before discharge' for incidental nodules.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes any outpatient referral order related to pulmonology or primary care follow-up satisfies this step and gets the case into the right downstream process.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes they mean the dedicated EHR order called 'Incidental Lung Nodule Follow-Up,' which uniquely populates the registry work queue.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: To both participants, 'put the order in' sounds like an obvious operational detail, so they treat it as settled without naming the exact EHR orderable or routing behavior.

turns.inner_thought: Three delayed lung cancer cases tied back to ED CTs is exactly the kind of thing that gets framed as an ED miss, when in these charts the abnormality was already on the imaging report. I need to keep this focused on a practical handoff fix, not create a huge new discharge burden for ED physicians. From my standpoint, if the team documented the finding, told the patient what follow-up was needed, and placed an outpatient referral, the loop should have been closed.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. As you know, the diagnostic safety review surfaced three delayed cancer cases involving incidental nodules first seen off ED imaging. I'd like us to walk through where the process broke down, because on paper we all thought these patients were being followed up and that the loop was getting closed.

turns.inner_thought: I need to show that the registry works when cases actually enter the pathway. I pulled the March nodule list by radiology finalization date, because that's how the registry operates, and none of those affected patients ever hit my queue. To me that means the loop was never truly closed at all.
turns.utterance: I reviewed the March nodule list on my side, and what stood out was that none of the affected patients ever reached the registry queue. So from where I sit, the follow-up pathway never really got activated for those March cases.

turns.inner_thought: She's probably talking about the same March ED discharges I reviewed. In those charts, the discharge notes did mention the nodules and advised follow-up, and in some cases there was already an outpatient referral. That means the ED team believed the handoff had happened. I need to make that clear without inviting blame.
turns.utterance: That's helpful, because when I looked at the March cases from the ED side, the discharge notes did include follow-up language. So at least at the point of discharge, it looked like the loop had been closed and the next step had been handed off.

turns.inner_thought: I should explain why my March list includes patients she may not be thinking of. Two of these were late-February ED visits, but the final radiology reads posted in early March, which is why they were on my March list. Either way, neither one was entered into the dedicated tracking pathway, so they were invisible to my team.
turns.utterance: One thing that may help reconcile the lists: two of the reports I'm looking at were final reads that posted in early March after late-February ED visits, so they still landed on the March nodule list for me. But in all of those cases, the patients were never entered for tracking, which is why nothing happened downstream.

turns.inner_thought: The patients I care most about are the ones any ED physician would see as dangerous: heavy smokers, prior cancer, concerning symptoms, weight loss, the people you'd never want to rely on a generic instruction for. If we can't build a perfect system for everyone right away, at minimum high-risk patients need a reliable capture process.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. My biggest concern is making sure the high-risk patients are captured every single time, because those are the cases where everyone would expect an extra layer of attention.

turns.inner_thought: I agree completely, though I'm thinking in terms of the guideline-defined high-risk category tied to surveillance recommendations. We had several 6 to 8 mm nodules in those higher-risk guideline buckets that never entered the program, and that's exactly what the registry is designed to prevent.
turns.utterance: I agree completely—high-risk patients should never be missed. And when I audited the recent cases, even several 6 to 8 millimeter nodules in high-risk categories never appeared in the nodule program, which is a real gap.

turns.inner_thought: We need a simple, low-friction ED step. If the radiology report recommends surveillance, the clinician can just place an outpatient referral before discharge and document that the patient was told what to do. That should standardize the handoff without piling on something elaborate.
turns.utterance: So maybe the immediate fix is straightforward: whenever the radiology report recommends surveillance, the ED team puts the order in before discharge. That gives us a clean standard step instead of relying on variable documentation.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—if they use the incidental lung nodule follow-up order, it will populate my registry queue and my team can take over outreach, reminders, and scheduling. That's the whole safety net. I'm glad she's on the same page about putting the order in.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that's the right direction. If the order goes in consistently, my team can work the queue and make sure the follow-up outreach happens, which is what we need to close the loop.

turns.inner_thought: This should be doable, because the ED already places plenty of PCP and pulmonology referrals. We can standardize that behavior around these incidental nodules rather than invent a whole new discharge workflow. As long as an outpatient referral is in, I consider that handed off out of the ED.
turns.utterance: Good. And from a feasibility standpoint, that should be manageable, because clinicians already place pulmonology or PCP referrals in a lot of these cases. We can standardize that step so putting the order in before discharge becomes routine.

turns.inner_thought: I'll watch next month's radiology-finalized March-style list and see whether more ED cases hit the registry once this new order step is in place. If they still don't appear, I'll send the misses back. I'm assuming the new discharge ordering step will route them correctly now.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll monitor next month's list and compare it against what reaches our queue, and I'll send back any misses so we can see whether the new discharge ordering step is improving things. If we do that consistently, I think we'll have a much better shot at closing the loop.
